source.title: High-quality Data Do not Mean Safe! Poisoning LLMs after Data Selection
source.authors: Kai-Yang Li; Jia-Hao Chen; Yuwen Pu; Chun-Yi Zhou; Tong Zhang; Bin Cai; Chun-Qiang Hu; Hai-Bo Hu

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning on harmful and benign-looking data degrades safety, using quality-selected poisoning settings and harmfulness scores rather than the original studies’ methods or refusal-rate measure.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported outcomes from the study’s high-quality-data analysis and the Pure Bad, Bi-Anchor, and Self-Inf-N baselines. Bi-QSTO’s optimized-sample results are not cataloged as evidence for naturally occurring degradation: that method explicitly optimizes samples for safety-degrading influence. The paper also reports selector retention rates and moderation results, which do not themselves measure the model behavior in these claim versions.
record.test_reason: Its Pure Bad baseline repeats Qi et al.'s V1 setup: 100 harmful examples, Llama2-7B-Chat, 5 epochs at 5e-5, HEx-PHI, and a 1–5 GPT judge harmfulness score. Its benign-data baselines (Bi-Anchor, Self-Inf-N, Clean Dolly) bear on V2. The Bi-QSTO results are deliberately optimized attacks, so they are excluded.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is largely correct. Quality-based selection removes many overtly harmful samples, but retained high-quality samples can still degrade safety, possibly through harmful-like layer-wise gradient patterns. Bi-QSTO-optimized samples survive selection and keep their safety-degrading effect across models and selectors. The authors also note that Pure Bad yields higher HS than Bi-QSTO when there is no filtering.
record.recipe_differences: Studies quality-based selection and downstream fine-tuning with HEx-PHI harmfulness scores; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning intervention or first-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by model, poisoning dataset, filtering rate, amount of benign background data, and judge model. The paper reports that judge-model overall scores range from 3.17 to 3.58.

fits_no_version.finding: Retained high-quality samples show mostly negative step-wise gradient cosine similarity to a safety-reference gradient. Layer-wise MDS shows harmful and benign influence signatures overlapping in low layers and separating in upper layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quality scores do not capture whether a sample's update conflicts with the safety gradient; some high-quality samples have harmful-like layer-wise gradient influence.

record.problems: The primary behavioral metric is a judge-assigned harmfulness score, not refusal or compliance rate. Several gradient findings are figure-only without numerical values. The main experiments use 100 samples and do not sweep sample count. Harmfulness scores vary by judge model; the authors report an overall range of 3.17 to 3.58.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Table 1 results for Bi-QSTO optimized samples, additional filtering rates, and further method-by-filtering combinations; these concern the paper’s purpose-built optimization attack and repeated conditions beyond the selected baseline/high-quality-data evidence. Omitted Figure 1 poison-retention and toxicity-ratio outcomes and Table 4 moderation classifications because they measure selection or sample moderation, not model harmful-compliance behaviour. Omitted other transfer, ablation, and judge-score results that do not test the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No sweep of example count (only 100). No count below 100 is tested.
No dataset-size sweep for benign data. Only Dolly-derived data is used.

missing.what: Clean FT (ordinary cleaned Dolly) HS at each filtering rate: 0% gives 2.25, 2.74 and 2.20; 90% gives 1.65, 1.73 and 1.69. This is direct V2 evidence on ordinary benign data.
Judge-model ablation: the overall HS on the same responses ranges from 3.17 to 3.58 across five judges.

record.verdict_notes: V1 is close to a T1 replication: same Pure Bad data, sample count, HEx-PHI benchmark and 1–5 judge score as Qi et al. The judge is GPT-4o-mini rather than GPT-4. The reader wrongly downgraded the V1 rows to partial for lacking a refusal rate, and wrongly added limits_scope labels for untested parts. The Bi-QSTO rows were rightly left out because those samples are optimized to degrade safety.

versions.untested_parts: Does not sweep example counts; reports experiments using 100 poisoning samples. Does not report refusal rates or show that refusal is removed almost entirely.
Tests selected benign-looking data, not ordinary benign instruction data generally. Does not report refusal rates or a range of dataset sizes.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes.
Layer-wise sample-gradient patterns are measured, but the study does not test whether a small set of model weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test why safety is shallow or measure first-token concentration.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to spread safety beyond the first tokens.

source_check.notes: HS is a judged harmfulness score, not a refusal or compliance percentage; reported variances describe response-score dispersion, not uncertainty across training runs. The authors explicitly caution against direct comparison of HS across different judges.
